'''''Sphaeropteris lepifera''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Cyathea lepifera''''', the '''brush pot tree''' ({{zh|c=筆筒樹|p=bǐtǒng shù}}; [[Japanese language|Japanese]]: ヒカゲヘゴ), or flying spider monkey tree fern is an [[endangered]] [[tree fern]] that grows in the mountains of East and [[Southeast Asia]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Steve Parker|title=Ferns, Mosses & Other Spore-Producing Plants|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GGhFoidwZhgC|year=2009|publisher=Capstone|isbn=978-0-7565-4220-7|page=4}}</ref> This species can grow up to {{convert|20|ft}} tall and 20 centimeters in diameter at the base.<ref name="dist1">{{cite journal |last1=Wei |first1=Xueying |last2=Harris |first2=Aj |last3=Cui |first3=Yuwen |last4=Dai |first4=Yangwu |last5=Hu |first5=Hanjia |last6=Yu |first6=Xiaoling |last7=Jiang |first7=Rihong |last8=Wang |first8=Faguo |title=Inferring the Potential Geographic Distribution and Reasons for the Endangered Status of the Tree Fern, ''Sphaeropteris lepifera'', in Lingnan, China Using a Small Sample Size |journal=Horticulturae |date=2021 |volume=7 |issue=11 |pages=496 |doi= 10.3390/horticulturae7110496 |doi-access=free }}</ref> While the tree fern lineage  dates back to the Jurassic, the crown group ''Sphaeropteris'' can be traced back to the Cretaceous, around 90 million years ago.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Sosa |first1=Victoria |last2=Ornelas |first2=Juan Francisco |last3=Ramírez-Barahona |first3=Santiago |last4=Gándara |first4=Etelvina |date=2016 |title=Historical reconstruction of climatic and elevation preferences and the evolution of cloud forest-adapted tree ferns in Mesoamerica |journal=PeerJ |volume=4 |at=[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5119233/figure/fig-1/ Chronogram of the Cyatheaceae and other tree fern lineages] |article-number=e2696 |doi=10.7717/peerj.2696 |doi-access=free |issn=2167-8359 |pmc=5119233 |pmid=27896030}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Korall | first1=Petra | last2=Pryer | first2=Kathleen M |date=2014 |title=Global biogeography of scaly tree ferns (Cyatheaceae): evidence for Gondwanan vicariance and limited transoceanic dispersal |journal=J. Biogeogr. |volume=41 | issue=2 |at=[https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4238398/] |doi= 10.1111/jbi.12222 |doi-access=free |pmid=25435648| pmc=4238398 | bibcode=2014JBiog..41..402K }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
This species can be found inhabiting moist [[subtropical]] and [[tropical rainforests]] in [[Japan]] ([[Ryukyu Islands]]), [[China]], [[Taiwan]], the [[Philippines]] and [[New Guinea]].<ref name="inat">{{cite web |title=Flying Spider Monkey Tree Fern (Sphaeropteris lepifera) |url=https://inaturalist.ca/taxa/460690-Sphaeropteris-lepifera |website=iNaturalist Canada |access-date=11 November 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Sphaeropteris lepifera (J.Sm. ex Hook.) R.M.Tryon {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:17531720-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Royal Botanical Gardens Kew |access-date=11 November 2025 |language=en}}</ref> In [[China]], the species can be found in coastal areas from [[Fujian]] to [[Guangxi]] along the South to [[Yunnan Province]].<ref name="inat" /> ''Sphaeropteris lepifera'' can also be found on [[Hainan]], along with an in-situ population being found in [[Nan'ao Island]] in [[Guangdong Province]].<ref name="dist1"/>

==Ecology==
Spores are generated bi-annually at the end of April and October. After a three-month process, sporophytes are formed by July/August or January/February depending on when the spores were generated. It has been found that low temperature and dry conditions result in decreased sporophyte production of ''S. lepifera''.<ref name="dist1"/>

==Conservation==
The rarity of ''Sphaeropteris lepifera'' within its natural range is believed to be contributed to by moisture levels.<ref name="dist1"/> This fern species prefers South facing slopes, which facilitate more sunlight for mature trees and provide shade for the [[fiddleheads]].<ref name="dist1"/> The species has motile sperm that require water to reach the female reproductive apparatus.<ref name="dist1"/> Moreover, in [[Taiwan]] and the peripheral [[Lanyu|Lanyu Township]], major die backs of tree ferns were reported in the mid 2000’s, believed to be caused by a new species of [[ascomycete fungus]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fu |first1=Chuen-Hsu |last2=Hsieh |first2=Huei-Mei |last3=Chen |first3=Chi-Yu |last4=Chang |first4=Tun-Tschu |last5=Huang |first5=Yao-Moan |last6=Ju |first6=Yu-Ming |title=''Ophiodiaporthe cyatheae'' gen. et sp. nov., a diaporthalean pathogen causing a devastating wilt disease of ''Cyathea lepifera'' in Taiwan |journal=Mycologia |date=1 July 2013 |volume=105 |issue=4 |pages=861–872 |doi=10.3852/12-346 |pmid=23709481 }}</ref>

==Uses==
''Sphaeropteris lepifera'' is valued in [[China]] medicinally. In the [[Philippines]], tree ferns are boiled, with the mixture containing boiling young fronds believed to help mothers reduce duration of labor and improve postpartum recovery.<ref name="raja">{{cite journal |last1=Rajapaksha |first1=Ranil |last2=Chamara |first2=Ruwan |last3=Huang |first3=Yao-Moan |last4=Ojha |first4=Rijan |last5=Pham |first5=Van The |last6=de Medeiros |first6=Caroline Modena |last7=Mustapeng |first7=Andi Maryani A. |last8=Coritico |first8=Fulgent |last9=Islam |first9=Taherul |last10=Coca |first10=Liuder Isidoro Rodríguez |last11=Bussmann |first11=Rainer W. |last12=Kamau |first12=Peris |title=Living with giant ferns: An ethnobotanical investigation of scaly tree ferns (Cyatheaceae) in a global context |journal=South African Journal of Botany |date=December 2024 |volume=175 |pages=453–469 |doi=10.1016/j.sajb.2024.10.037 |bibcode=2024SAJB..175..453R }}</ref> 
[[Image:Cyathea lepifera cooked.jpg|thumb|left|The fern cooked in plum sauce]][[Starch]] in the stems of ''Sphaeropteris lepifera'' are also valued for food within [[China]] and [[Taiwan]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Liu |first1=Yujing |last2=Wujisguleng |first2=Wujisguleng |last3=Long |first3=Chunlin |title=Food uses of ferns in China: a review |journal=Acta Societatis Botanicorum Poloniae |date=2012 |volume=81 |issue=4 |pages=263–270 |doi=10.5586/asbp.2012.046 |bibcode=2012AcSBP..81..263L |doi-access=free }}</ref> In [[Japan]], the new leaves and shoots are consumed. They are boiled to remove bitterness and then eaten as tempura or pickled in vinegar (sanbaizu); the texture is said to be like that of a [[daikon radish]]. The boiled core of ''Sphaeropteris lepifera'' is also a festival food in the [[Yaeyama Islands]] and [[Ishigaki Island]]. 
In [[Taiwan]] and the [[Philippines]], it is possible to find sculptures and construction material made of tree fern trunk.<ref name="raja"/>
